title: Paranormal Activity
wpTitle: Paranormal Activity West End Reviews Round-up – Ambassadors Theatre London

ratings.excerpt: This fright night leaves you spellbound and spooked … With expert direction and eye-catching stagecraft, the tension is ramped up in a play inspired by the film franchise … By treating horror as an art form rather than a cheap set of jump scares, this thrilling new show, which wears its connection to the world of the Paranormal Activity film franchise lightly, proves how jaw-clenchingly, arm-clutchingly frightening horror on stage can be. … Under the direction of Punchdrunk’s Felix Barrett, the in-the-moment fear is acute. But what is remarkable, thanks to Chris Fisher’s eye-popping illusions, is how that terror is accompanied by a giddy, awe-filled delight at the devilry we just witnessed – and how the hell they made it work. … The script may be perfunctory, and some of it is deeply hammy

This West End stage outing for the horror franchise is shockingly good … ... in some ways the fact that Fly Davis’s set is nothing but the couple’s mundane two-storey house captures the genre’s claustrophobia nicely: did something just move in that corner? … We’ve been asked not to spoiler, so I won’t, but key to the production – even more so than Levi Holloway’s smartly constructed script – is that it’s directed by Felix Barrett from immersive legends Punchdrunk. He practically wrote the book on creepily atmospheric theatre … There’s some pretty jaw-dropping stuff I’d best not even obliquely describe. But on the whole it avoids manipulative jump scares in favour of unnerving moments of rug pulling … Again, it’s not Shakespeare: Holloway’s dialogue is shallow in terms of characterisation,

This play is as terrifying as the film … Immersive theatre pioneers Punchdrunk bring all the jumpscares of the cult movie about a young couple hounded by ghosts to the Ambassadors Theatre in London … ... Felix Barrett, Punchdrunk’s pioneer of underworldly immersive theatre, who here deploys a full range of disorientating, rationality-defying effects to summon the terror wattage of the original. … Where the scariest moments of the film lie in recorded footage, here Barrett leans fully into the live experience, and it pays off. … As the evening builds the shrieks intensify with shower curtains or doors opened to investigate the causes of unexplained noises. … Chris Fisher’s stunning illusions prove the coup de grâce, challenging the pelvic floor as much as the mind. The scariest show on the West End? … Punchdrunk director Felix Barrett conjures frights aplenty with this stage adaptation of the supernatural film franchise … If you enjoy the deliciously creepy feeling of your hair stirring on your tightening scalp in anticipation of terror, Paranormal Activity is the show for you. … ... Barrett uses the full armoury of stage frights, from crash blackouts and sudden blaring rock music, to jump scares wrought through sound and lighting effects, to put the willies up us. A thrilling theatrical take on the horror movie franchise … Punchdrunk’s Felix Barrett creates an unsettling, often terrifying show at the Ambassadors Theatre, London … ... now here is Felix Barrett, best known as the pioneering director of immersive Punchdrunk shows, with a brilliantly terrifying stage response to the popular Paranormal Activity film franchise. … Theatre, of course, doesn’t have the same special effects at its disposal as the screen. But it does have something even more powerful: the audience’s imagination responding in real time. … Barrett and writer Levi Holloway make ingenious use of that fact. Truly terrifying experience … Stage version of the hit supernatural horror franchise is a nerve-shredding success … The chills of the big screen are expertly translated to the stage by writer Levi Holloway and director Felix Barrett in this story set in the supernatural world of the hit Paranormal Activity horror film franchise. … Holloway has wisely shorn his play of the increasingly elaborate demonic mythology of Oren Peli’s found-footage film series. … Shifting the story to a rainy UK isn’t just a way to appeal to British audiences; it also cleverly serves to further isolate the couple in a place where nothing is fully familiar. Holloway also takes his time to build up the complexities of James and Lou’s relationship … Heusinger nicely shades in the narcissism and golden-boy entitlement
